title: Anisotropic KV & Attention field notes
content:
Quick brain dump after skim + three paper deep-dives (Dec 5-8, 2026). Goal: capture ideas that could translate into low-risk experiments on Redwood serving runtime (small perf wins for long-context workloads). Notes are rough; actionable items at bottom.

Why this cluster of papers matters to Redwood: increasing model context length + tighter latency/cost budgets means we need smarter KV management and attention sparsity that the runtime can exploit without model retraining. Papers below propose anisotropic/heterogeneous KV layouts, learned importance scores, and cheap eviction/compaction schemes — all promising for Dedicated and Private customers who care about long sessions.

Papers skimmed (order = depth):
- "Anisotropic Attention for Efficient Long Context" (arXiv 2026) — main idea: allow attention kernel to vary per head and per token group (dense for recent tokens, low-rank for far tokens). Implementation note: requires attention masks + two execution modes.
- "KV Compression via Learned Quantization & Delta-encoding" (NeurIPS 2025 follow-up) — compress KV frames online using lightweight delta encoding with periodic rebase. Quality loss small for informational tokens.
- "Stamped Evictions: workload-aware KV pruning" (workshop 2026) — heuristic policy using token-level salience + recency; cheap to compute, robust across domains.
- "Latent Prefix Stitching" (short paper) — store compressed prefix representations and stitch on-demand when long-range retrieval needed.

Key takeaways and reproduction ideas:
1) Anisotropic attention seems implementable inside the runtime without model surgery: treat attention as two-tiered compute path. For compatible model artifacts we can provide a shim that rewrites attention masks + switches kernel per token range. Potential quick experiment: emulate anisotropic behavior by post-processing logits with learned decay on kv-similarity (no retrain) to approximate low-rank far attention.

2) KV compression + delta-encoding: low CPU overhead if we use int8 deltas and occasional fp16 rebase. Good candidate for Dedicated where GP memory pressure matters. Danger: serialization/deserialization cost at inference path — measure end-to-end. Experiment: integrate a minimal delta layer into our KV store in a feature-flagged branch and benchmark throughput/latency with long-context demo (8k / 32k tokens).

3) Stamped evictions (salience score) mixes well with our automatic prefix caching. Implementation is embarrassingly parallel: compute salience score for each token on generation (cheap heuristics: noun-phrase presence, entity markers, user-labeled flags). Start with simple heuristic: weighted sum of recency & token-importance estimated by token logit surprise.

4) Latent stitching is attractive for chat apps that preserve semantic state but not verbatim tokens. More research needed on what gets lost when compressing prefixes; likely safe for systems prompts and generic chit-chat.

Open questions / cautions:
- How much overhead do multi-path attention kernels add to small-batch latency? For PLG-hosted API we cannot degrade p99. Might be better as Dedicated-only or opt-in.
- Stability across languages/emoji/code tokens: heuristics might fail on code-heavy sessions. Need domain split in benchmarks.
- Observable failure modes: quality regressions for factual recall when we compress/rewrite KVs. Must tie to evals (prompt sets) before rollout.

Actionable next steps (rapid experiment plan):
A) "Aniso-sim" proof-of-concept (2 engineer-days): implement a post-attention weighting shim that decays similarity for far tokens to approximate low-rank. Canary on a small model (7B) with synthetic long-context benchmark. Metrics: token-level perplexity, answer-F1 on retrieval QA, p50/p95 latency.

B) "Delta-KV" PoC (3-4 engineer-days): add a simple delta-compressor to the KV store (int8 deltas + periodic fp16 checkpoint). Evaluate compression ratio, CPU overhead, and effect on throughput for 16k/32k sessions.

C) "Stamped-evict" scheduler (1-2 days): add salience score plug-in into existing eviction path; run A/B on internal chat workload. Track number of evicted tokens, quality regressions (via held prompts), cost savings.

Notes-to-self for benchmarking:
- Build prompts that mix factual retrieval, instruction-following, and code to stress different token semantics.
- Use Replay harness (GH link above) + perf runner to capture p50/p90/p99.
- Add eval probes that check hallucination rate after compression.

Potential integration plan for Redwood product tiers:
- Hosted API: only safe, read-only experiments that do not risk p99 increase; prefer post-processing approximations and offline compression for cold storage.
- Dedicated: opt-in compression & anisotropic kernels as config flags; provide cost/latency hints in Console.
- Private: allow full feature set with audit logs, rebase schedules, and KMS integration for serialized KV states.

Random ideas to file away:
- Learn a tiny adapter that predicts token-level salience (cheap MLP on top of last hidden) and run it at generation time. Could be distilled and run on CPU as a heuristic.
- Use model's own attention scores (head-level) to decide which heads to run densely vs approx (head pruning on the fly).

References to collect (todo):
- full arXiv PDFs + supplementary tests
- any open-source kernels for low-rank attention (RFA, Performer variants)
- related GH experiments inside Redwood (link to kv-experiments issue above)

To follow up: schedule 30-min sync with Mira + Ethan to decide which PoC to prioritize (aiming for small win we can demo to infra/product in 2 weeks).

End of notes.
